## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Three goals today. You understand the concept of tidy data. You get an overview
over the most common transformation routines. And you master a number of
functions from the tidyr and dplyr packages to address some of these challenges.

This session is the direct continuation of the data-import session: there we got
the data into R, here we bring it into the shape we actually want.

## Slide 4 · The role of data preparation

The same picture as last time: data preparation and processing, visualisation,
and analysis and modelling feed into each other, and everything funnels into the
presentation of the insights as one overall story.

Last time we dealt with the import step. Today we deal with what happens
immediately afterwards, and where — realistically — you will spend most of your
time in any empirical project.

## Slide 5 · The goal: tidy data

Hadley Wickham, who wrote most of the packages we use today, opened his paper on
tidy data with this sentence, and it is a good summary of the situation.

Translated into plain English: we find data sets in all kinds of messed-up forms
in the world, and we must turn them into a form that is a good starting point for
any further task.

The good thing is that this target form is unique. There are infinitely many ways
for a data set to be messy, but only one way for it to be tidy — so you always
know what you are aiming at, even when you have no idea yet how to get there.

## Slide 6 · Three demands

Three demands define tidy data, and they are worth memorising literally.

Every row corresponds to one and only one observation. Every column corresponds
to one and only one variable. And every cell corresponds to one and only one
value.

Every data set that satisfies these three demands is called tidy. It is an
excellent start for basically every further task — but note the caveat: it is
maybe not the best way to represent data to humans. A tidy table is often long
and repetitive, and for a printed table in a paper you will frequently convert it
back into something wider.

## Slide 7 · Three ways to be untidy

Each of the three demands can be violated separately, and it is worth being able
to name which one is broken.

On the left, a row holds two observations, because the years sit in separate
columns. In the middle, there is a column called `variable` whose entries are
variable names rather than values. On the right, a single cell contains several
values — industry names and percentages mixed into one string.

The third one is the nastiest in practice, because you cannot compute with it at
all until you have split it apart, and splitting text reliably is genuinely hard.

The goal of data wrangling is to turn such untidy data into tidy data.

## Slide 8 · Recap questions

Four recap questions. The third one is the interesting one and the answer is yes:
for presentation. A table in a paper, or a table you hand to a colleague, is
usually more readable in wide format. The rule is that tidy is the working
format, not necessarily the publication format.

## Slide 10 · The way to tidy data

Since the starting point to tidy data is always different but the goal is always
the same, the steps are also always the same: six main routines, which you
combine in whatever order the particular mess requires.

Two main packages are relevant. tidyr provides functions for reshaping data into
tidy format, which is what people usually mean by wrangling. And dplyr provides
functions for manipulating data in order to extract the information you want.

Keep that division in mind — it tells you which package's documentation to open.

## Slide 11 · 1. Reshaping: long ⇄ wide

The first routine is reshaping data from wide to long format and back.

On the left the wide version: one column per variable. On the right the long
version: one column holding the variable names and one holding the values.

Note that neither is inherently tidy — it depends on what an observation is
supposed to be in your analysis. If your unit of observation is a
country-year-indicator triple, the long form is tidy; if it is a country-year,
the wide form is.

The two functions are `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()` from tidyr.

## Slide 12 · 2. Filter rows · 3. Select columns

Routines two and three, and they are the pair that beginners mix up most often.

`filter()` keeps rows that satisfy a condition — here only the German
observations. `select()` keeps columns — here we drop unemployment.

The mnemonic that helps: filter answers "which observations?", select answers
"which variables?". Note also the double equals sign in the filter condition: a
single equals sign would be an assignment and gives you an error.

## Slide 13 · 4. Mutate · 5. Group and summarise

Routine four is mutating: adding a new variable that is computed from existing
ones. The number of rows stays the same.

Routine five is grouping and summarising: you declare which variable defines the
groups and then compute one number per group. Here the four country-year rows
collapse into two country rows.

The crucial difference, and this comes back as an exam question: `mutate()` keeps
the number of rows and adds a column; `summarise()` reduces the number of rows to
the number of groups.

## Slide 14 · 6. Merge several data sets

The sixth routine is merging several data sets, which in practice you need
constantly: GDP comes from one source, emissions from another.

The joining functions differ only in which rows survive when the two data sets do
not match perfectly. `left_join()` keeps all rows of the left data set,
`right_join()` all of the right, `full_join()` all of both, and `inner_join()`
only those present in both.

Two practical warnings. First, always join on *all* the columns that identify an
observation — here country and year, not only country. Second, check the number
of rows before and after: an unexpected increase means your join keys were not
unique.

## Slide 15 · The six routines at a glance

Here they are together. After having imported your data into R, you can usually
make it tidy using a sequential combination of these six routines.

That is a genuinely encouraging claim: the space of things you have to learn is
small and closed. What varies is the order and the number of steps, not the
vocabulary.

This way you produce the inputs we used for visualisation, and the inputs we will
use for modelling.

## Slide 16 · Recap questions

Four recap questions on part two. Work through them in pairs before we move to
the practical part — if you cannot name the six routines from memory, the
practice afterwards will be much harder than it needs to be.

## Slide 18 · Short recap on reshaping

We go through the routines via direct demonstration, starting with reshaping.

Take `data_raw_long.csv`, which has a variable column and a value column, and
make it wider so that Germany and Greece each get their own column. Then take
`data_raw_wide.csv`, which has the years as columns, and make it longer so that
you get a year column and a gini column.

Watch the type of the `year` column after pivoting longer: it comes out as
character, because it used to be a column *name*. You will usually want to
convert it back to integer.

## Slide 19 · Short recap on manipulation basics

Five steps on the wine data set, and they exercise filter, select and mutate in
combination.

Step two is worth a comment: after filtering to white wines only, the column
`kind` contains the same value in every row and therefore carries no information
any more — which is exactly why you remove it.

Step five needs a little thought: "the highest quality score" is not a fixed
number, so you need something like `filter(quality == max(quality))`.

## Slide 20 · Short recap on summarising and grouping

The opening question is the conceptual one from earlier: mutate keeps all rows
and adds a column, summarise collapses rows into groups.

Task one needs `group_by(kind)` followed by `summarise()`. Task two is
deliberately the other case: you want one value per wine, so it is a `mutate()`,
and inside it you compare each wine's quality to `mean(quality)` over the whole
data set.

Doing both back to back is the fastest way to internalise the difference.

## Slide 21 · Short recap on joining data sets

Three joining tasks. Run the same join with all four functions and compare the
number of rows and the pattern of NAs — that comparison teaches the concept
faster than any explanation.

The last question is the important one in practice. Joining only on `id` when the
data also varies over time produces every combination of matching rows, so your
data set can grow dramatically and silently. If a join unexpectedly multiplies
your rows, this is almost always the reason.

## Slide 23 · Pipes

While not strictly necessary, you can improve the usability and readability of
your code using so-called pipes.

Pipes take the result from their left and throw it to the right. The thrown
result can be referred to via a dot, and by default it is used as the first
argument of the function in the next line — which is why you can usually leave
the dot out entirely.

Compare the two versions on the slide: they do exactly the same thing. The right
one reads as "take data_raw, then select these columns", which is much closer to
how you think about the operation.

## Slide 24 · Pipes: a practical example

A more practical example: two reshaping steps, once with named intermediate
objects and once as one pipe chain.

The piped version is shorter and it puts the desired stage at the end, so you
read it as a recipe.

But note the advice at the bottom, which is the genuinely useful part: while
developing code it is usually easier to make the intermediate steps explicit. If
a chain of six piped steps produces the wrong result, you cannot inspect the
middle of it. Write it with intermediate objects first, check each one, and pipe
it together afterwards if you like.

## Slide 25 · Recap on piping

Four questions on pipes. The second one has no single right answer, and that is
the point — argue for your position. My own answer is on the previous slide:
explicit first, piped afterwards.

For the last point, note that R now also has a native pipe written `|>`, which
does not require any package. You will meet both in code you find online; they
behave the same way for our purposes.

## Slide 26 · Tidy selection helpers

It can become tedious to select many columns using explicit reference to their
names — imagine a data set with forty indicator columns.

The tidy selection helpers let you select columns based on common criteria:
`starts_with()`, `ends_with()`, `contains()`, `all_of()` and several others.

And they combine: wrap several selectors in `c()` and you get their union, as in
the example on the right.

One note on `all_of()`: it errors if a named column does not exist, which is a
feature — it means a typo or a renamed column fails loudly instead of silently
selecting nothing.

## Slide 27 · Exercise 1: filtering and reshaping

The first real exercise. Import `exercise_1.csv`, keep only Greece and Germany
between 1995 and 2015, make it wider so that gdp and co2 become their own
columns, and save the result in `data/tidy/`.

Note the target output: 42 rows — two countries times twenty-one years. Checking
that number is a good habit; if you get 84, your filter did not work, and if you
get 21, you lost a country.

And remember from the import session: save into `data/tidy`, never back into
`data/raw`.

## Slide 28 · Exercise 2: mutating, selecting & summarising

The second exercise combines select, mutate, filter and summarise in one chain —
which is what a real preparation script looks like.

Work out the order for yourself: does it matter whether you filter the years
before or after computing the averages? It does, and getting that wrong is the
classic mistake. Filtering after summarising would average over all years first
and then throw rows away.

The bonus asks for a bar plot of the CO2 averages, which connects back to the
visualisation session and gives you a visual check on whether the numbers are
plausible.

## Slide 29 · Summary

To summarise: after importing raw data you usually must prepare them, which means
making them tidy. Tidy data is the input to any visualisation or modelling task,
and it is defined by the three demands we have now seen several times.

The practical advice in the middle is the one to take away: write one script that
imports raw data and saves tidy data. That single script is what makes the
distance between `data/raw` and `data/tidy` reproducible — and it is what you
hand to anybody who wants to check your work.

## Slide 30 · The functions, and what they are for

And here are the six routines mapped onto the actual function names. This slide
is the one to keep open while doing the exercises.

In later sessions we will also learn about some convenience shortcuts that
combine several of these steps.

The last line is not a platitude: data preparation is mainly about practice.
Nobody learns wrangling by reading about wrangling — you learn it by being stuck
on a specific messy file and getting unstuck. So do the exercises, and bring the
problems you hit to the Moodle forum.
